title: The State of Longevity | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z Bio + Health argues longevity has gone mainstream after COVID and ChatGPT, with value shifting to an 'action layer' (healthcare-home apps, testing-to-treatment, wearables). A 500-person US survey backs six trends: non-toxic spending (62% pay more), peptides (gray market single-digit billions vs ~$44B tirzepatide in 9M 2026), cholesterol and Lp(a), third-gen wearables, and consumer neurotech.

themes.theme: Healthcare home and the action layer

insights.claim: Consumer health is converging on a race to build a single 'healthcare home' app combining records, labs and imaging, wearable data, AI interpretation and access to clinicians. Contenders are Function Health, Oura, WHOOP, General Medicine, Counsel, Ferry Health, and OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon and Apple.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Mapping which head start (data, daily habit, care delivery, distribution) wins is the key diligence question for consumer health.
insights.locator: The race to become a healthcare home

insights.claim: As AI makes health answers and interpretation cheaper, value migrates to whoever owns the action layer: ordering tests, booking appointments, follow-up care and prescriptions.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Pure AI Q&A health products are commoditizing; defensibility sits in fulfillment and clinical workflow integration.
insights.quote: As AI makes answers and interpretation cheaper, value will migrate to the companies that can figure out the action layer.

insights.claim: Generalist AI assistants are unlikely to prioritize healthcare's messy complexity, leaving room for very large vertical companies; the same complexity makes the category hard to build but also hard to replace. a16z expects multiple winners.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Argues against the view that frontier labs absorb consumer health; incumbent-complexity moat is the bet.

insights.claim: Awareness of microplastics is now mainstream: 63% of surveyed US consumers are aware of them, 35% are concerned, and the most extreme biohackers try plasma exchange to remove them from blood.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Microplastics are a durable consumer-concern theme, from mainstream filtering to fringe interventions.
insights.locator: From organic food to non-toxic everything

insights.claim: Surveyed Americans are changing household habits: 70% filter water, 39% swap plastic for glass, 24% use nontoxic cookware, 37% buy air purifiers, 18% test for mold, 17.5% buy organic-cotton clothing or bedding, 11% buy natural mattresses, and 14% try to reduce EMF.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Water filtration is already majority behavior; the long tail (mattresses, EMF) is early.

insights.claim: 62% of respondents would pay more for products labeled 'non-toxic', and a16z concedes consumer spending is moving faster than the evidence, so willingness to pay rests on peace of mind rather than measurable health benefit.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Premium pricing for 'clean' labels is demand-led and could be vulnerable to regulatory or scientific pushback.
insights.quote: Consumer spending is moving faster than the evidence.

insights.claim: The MAHA movement has pushed toxins in food, water and everyday products into public view, driving growth in willingness to spend on clean products.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Policy and political tailwinds support the non-toxic category across food, home goods and personal care.

themes.theme: Peptides: regulated pharma vs gray market

insights.claim: The compounded or unregulated peptide market is single-digit billions, dwarfed by Eli Lilly's tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound), which generated nearly $44 billion in sales in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Gray-market peptide enthusiasm is small next to approved GLP-1 economics; value remains with regulated drugs.

insights.claim: GLP-1 success, comfort with self-injection and loosening regulation are fueling consumer experimentation with non-FDA-approved peptides such as BPC-157 (repair) and melanotan II (tanning), with thin human safety and efficacy data and supplier-quality risk. HHS policy now eases enforcement on pharmacies compounding six peptides.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Regulatory easing is a catalyst but also a tail risk for the gray-market segment.
insights.quote: the market’s enthusiasm to date has outpaced the actual evidence

insights.claim: Biotech: a16z predicts a growing pipeline of rigorous FDA-regulated peptide drugs, with investors underwriting medicines that also have vast consumer appeal. Consumer pull creates an unusually efficient path to patients, which could extend to sleep, bone health and cardiovascular health.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Consumer demand pull is an underweighted factor when valuing peptide-drug pipelines.

insights.claim: Care delivery may repeat the GLP-1 cycle: dedicated prescribing startups first (like Calibrate, Found, Weekend Health), then incumbents adding peptides. Value mostly accrued to pharma last time, and as prescribing commoditizes it becomes a retention tool rather than an acquisition tool.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Expect pharma, not telehealth prescribers, to capture most economics of the next peptide wave.

themes.theme: Cholesterol and cardiovascular risk going mainstream

insights.claim: Evidence increasingly supports 'lower is better' for LDL, particularly in high-risk people. An October study found intensive treatment shrank coronary plaque by about a fifth over 18 months in people with heart disease, so 'normal' LDL may not be enough.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Supports an expanded addressable market for lipid-lowering therapy beyond standard targets.

insights.claim: Only 21% of survey respondents knew of PCSK9 inhibitors like Repatha. a16z expects them to enter the consumer zeitgeist as miracle cholesterol drugs, helped by Lipfendra, the first daily-pill PCSK9 inhibitor, FDA-approved in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: An oral PCSK9 removes the injection barrier and could widen use; awareness is the gap.

insights.claim: In people with diabetes and no known major artery disease, adding Repatha lowered estimated five-year risk of first heart attack, stroke or coronary death from 7.1% to 5.0%, supporting treatment before a first event.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Primary-prevention evidence widens the eligible population for PCSK9 therapy.

insights.claim: Lp(a), an inherited risk factor affecting roughly one in five people and largely unaffected by diet or exercise, is the next frontier. US guidelines now recommend testing once in adulthood. Novartis's pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) but missed its primary cardiovascular-events endpoint, while a16z stays optimistic on Eli Lilly and Amgen candidates.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Clinical benefit of Lp(a) lowering remains unproven; the Lilly and Amgen readouts are key binary catalysts.

insights.claim: A startup opportunity exists in connecting testing (including Lp(a)) to personalized treatment, medication access and progress tracking, since knowing your numbers is only the starting point.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Action-oriented cardiology services layered on diagnostics fit the broader action-layer thesis.
insights.quote: The opportunity is helping people act on them.

insights.claim: 54% of surveyed consumers use a wearable and 83% of those check it daily, yet 55% say their data never prompted a behavior change or doctor's visit, and nearly three in four would wear a second device if it measured something new.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Engagement is high but actionability is low; new biomarkers, not more of the same, drive the next device purchase.

insights.claim: Wearables are in a third generation: Fitbit counted steps, Oura, WHOOP and Apple Watch made sleep and recovery routine, and now Clair (hormone patterns without blood draw) and Lumia (blood-flow in earrings) answer specific health questions.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: A clean generational framework for screening new wearable startups by the question they answer.

insights.claim: Deregulation is aiding wearables: in January 2026 the FDA updated its general wellness policy for non-invasive wearables, and in June it closed its warning letter to WHOOP after it changed its Blood Pressure Insights feature and labeling. Oura also offers blood-pressure-related wellness insights.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Regulatory room expands only within wellness-claim boundaries; claim creep is the risk.

insights.claim: The bigger prize is an unobtrusive device tracking a wide range of biomarkers in real time, such as a non-invasive CGM measuring far more than glucose, which would make step trackers feel archaic.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Multi-analyte non-invasive sensing is the high-risk, high-payoff frontier.

insights.claim: Implantable BCI progress: Neuralink lets paralyzed trial participants control computers by decoding motor cortex activity, and is developing visual cortex stimulation for blindness. UCSF's Edward Chang uses surface electrode arrays, decoded full words in 2021 and more recently speech and gestures together.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Surface-recording approaches may offer a safer long-term path than penetrating implants.

insights.claim: Non-invasive neural decoding is being approached as a data scaling problem: Conduit, Alljoined and Aleph Neuro collect large datasets to train AI models that translate noisy signals into text and images, potentially enabling communication with AI agents without words.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Scaling-law logic applied to neural data; unproven signal quality is the central risk.

insights.claim: Neuro wearables are moving from 'read' to 'write', using targeted brain or peripheral-nerve stimulation to improve sleep and focus. a16z bets that BCIs and brain wearables become a real consumer category in our lifetimes.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Stimulation-based sleep and focus devices are the nearest commercial entry point.
insights.quote: we’re betting in our lifetimes, brain-computer interfaces and “wearables” for the brain will become a real consumer category

insights.claim: Survey interest in consumer neurotech: 39% would use a non-invasive brain-sensing device for sleep, focus or mood and 29% for thought-controlled devices, with greater interest among men.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Stated interest is moderate and skewed male; stated intent overstates purchases.

insights.claim: Mainstreaming of hands-on health management was accelerated by COVID-19 (exposing the limits of the medical system) and by ChatGPT, which let anyone interpret medical information in plain English.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Two shocks, mortality awareness and AI literacy, underpin durable consumer health spending.

insights.claim: a16z's framing for founders: the biggest longevity opportunities go to companies that help people take action and manage health over time. Start with a problem consumers care about, prove it helps, make it easy to keep using, and grow with the customer.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Signals where a16z Bio + Health will deploy: retention-oriented action and management products rather than information.
insights.quote: We think some of the biggest opportunities in longevity will go to companies that help people take action and manage their health over time.

insights.claim: a16z's survey of 500 randomly selected US consumers shows they are seeking tests, trying new products and spending their own money on health; sample is small and self-reported.
insights.speaker: Daisy Wolf, Eva Steinman
insights.so_what: Treat survey percentages as directional, not precise market sizing.
